title: Connected and disconnected graphs: all vertices reachable vs. an isolated vertex
summary: Compare connectivity when all five vertices are mutually reachable versus when an isolated vertex is present.
context: Both the left and right figures show undirected graphs with vertices 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. An undirected graph is "connected" if starting from any vertex, every other vertex can be reached along a path of one or more edges; it does not require a direct edge between every pair of vertices.
description: On the left is "Connected graph (All vertices are mutually reachable)" with seven undirected edges: 1—2, 1—3, 1—5, 2—3, 2—4, 2—5, and 4—5. Even though vertices 3 and 4 have no direct edge, they can reach each other along path 3—2—4 or 3—1—5—4, so all five vertices form a single connected whole.

On the right is "Disconnected graph (Some vertices are unreachable from others)": it keeps the five undirected edges 1—2, 1—3, 1—5, 2—3, and 2—5 among the four vertices on the left, while removing the two edges 2—4 and 4—5 incident to vertex 4. Vertices 1, 2, 3, 5 remain mutually reachable among themselves, whereas no path reaches the isolated vertex 4 in the right figure.

frames.title: Connected and disconnected graphs: all vertices reachable vs. an isolated vertex
frames.explanation: The right graph splits into the connected subset {1, 2, 3, 5} and the isolated vertex {4}. Whenever at least one pair of vertices cannot reach each other along a path, the entire undirected graph is disconnected.
